Kate Compton's Chancery models chatbots as finite state machines, like an old board game with instructions written on its spaces, combined with an internal blackboard and Tracery text generation; her kitten simulator moves between idle, hungry and angry states on timers and counts how many pets it tolerates before biting ([Various 2018, 29:35](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1775)). Diarytown, led by Melanie Dickinson and described by Max Kreminski (whose "gardening" mode of play appears earlier), has players compose diary entries about their real lives from Lego-like action blocks, then runs sifting patterns to renarrativize their life in a magical-realist tone; Kreminski calls it a step toward malleable simulation, where players shape their computational story partner through play ([Max Kreminski 2019, 23:08](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1388)).

At the far edge, the generator is alive. Julian Day describes Christian Bök's Xenotext, which uses bacteria as a procedural generator: a poem encoded into a gene is expressed by the organism to produce a second poem, aiming for a poem that outlasts humanity ([Julian Day 2020, 20:02](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=1202)). It worked in E. coli, but the extremophile host quickly undid the gene, raising an open question about stopping evolution from changing a generative artwork; Bök has worked on it since 2002 and spent over $100,000 ([Julian Day 2020, 24:45](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=1485)). Cassie Stuurman's slime molds are another biological algorithm: they solve mazes by filling the space and shrinking to the shortest path between food sources, and avoid places marked by their own residue, a spatial memory that lets them escape a U-shaped trap used to test robot navigation ([Cassie Stuurman 2017, 7:26](https://youtu.be/LoPxtQq0ut4?t=446)).

### Generative thinking beyond art

Two talks apply the roguelike's combinatorial lens to life and mathematics. Andrew Cedotal argues that as the space of self-improvement options grows, more success stories will come from acquiring apparently unrelated skills that only later combine, so that life feels more about searching than struggling, and finding out whether they combine takes years of high-risk commitment ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 22:09](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=1329)). He frames Luca Galante's creation of Vampire Survivors as one such career combo: a taste for Ultima Online's chaotic low-res real-time 2D, digging through obscure mobile games, and experience making slot machines ([Andrew Cedotal 2024, 13:38](https://youtu.be/Gxn_MA3-Vgo?t=818)). Nat Alison, in the same talk in which she describes teaching maths as discovery, shows the generative experiment in its simplest form: plotting successive pairs of Fibonacci numbers modulo various bases produced unexpected crosses and fractal shapes, and she later found the cross appears whenever the modulus is itself a Fibonacci number ([Nat Alison 2024, 19:37](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=1177)).

**In practice:**

- Decide whether your generator is meant to finish the work or to provoke a person. A provocation can be crude; it only needs to move the human off their habits ([Clarissa Littler 2020, 10:00](https://youtu.be/OzCGTXakbjE?t=600); [Max Hawkins 2019, 7:59](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=479)).
- Start with a single drop of randomness. Fix the categories of material and randomise their relationships before reaching for more ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 2:34](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=154); [Chelsea Thompto 2026, 4:47](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=287)).
- Expect a curation step after the random one, by the maker or the audience ([Max Hawkins 2019, 28:26](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=1706); [Botnik 2017, 2:16](https://youtu.be/IujSOW1OMWk?t=136)).
- If the output is meant to be a finished puzzle, watch for sameness of solution: varied grids solved the same way are not variety ([Nat Alison 2023, 2:14](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=134)).
- For a work that keeps generating, keep it recognisably the same work and let the contents change ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 3:11](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=191)).

## Tensions and open questions

### Which roguelike element does a purpose need?

The cases in this chapter keep different parts of the skeleton. *Love Island* keeps both the run and permanent loss ([Florence Smith Nicholls 2023, 2:18](https://youtu.be/MQw3pe-z6JM?t=138)). Gillian Smith's WPI keeps the runs but removes permanent failure, because its aim is to get people to take risks ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:02:05](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=3725)). Stephen Ware's police trainer keeps repetition and permadeath but removes randomness, so a trainee can change one action and see its effect ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 18:41](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1121)). Nuzlocke players go the other way and add permanent loss to games that lack it ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:47:24](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31644)). None of these is the correct roguelike; the choice depends on what the activity is for: learning through risk wants runs without lasting loss, isolating cause and effect wants repetition without variation, and challenge and attachment want loss. Vermilion leaves open exactly which Nuzlocke ideas roguelikes should take ([Stella Vermilion 2026, 8:49:34](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=31774)).

### Distil the source genre or change its feel?

*Against the Storm* keeps the opening hours of a city builder's loop and compresses them into a run ([Aron Pietroń and Michał Ogłoziński 2023, 2:28](https://youtu.be/tWFIQaeSs6M?t=148)). Josh Grams and Brian Walker instead change the source genre's tempo, making flight turn-based so players can experiment, or freezing a platformer's time so play stays cerebral ([Josh Grams 2020, 0:25](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=25); [Brian Walker 2018, 20:40](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1240)). The choice depends on whether the source genre's feel is the attraction or the barrier. Tyriq Plummer's recipe metaphor and his own Vagante and Catacomb Kids comparison also pull apart: a hybrid can be described by proportions, yet two games with nearly the same borrowed features feel completely different ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 4:32](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=272); [Tyriq Plummer 2017, 14:57](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=897)). And Alexander King's set-based card acquisition remains untested, because no hit has used it yet ([Alexander King 2025, 15:27](https://youtu.be/uwiFwic03EE?t=927)).

### Farming or gardening?

Tabea Iseli borrowed from farming games because they share the roguelite's loop of resources, priorities and goals across runs ([Tabea Iseli 2024, 3:29](https://youtu.be/-MX1imoSxTg?t=209)). Max Kreminski worries that value extraction is what makes a game "farming" rather than "gardening", and says he cannot yet draw the line between them ([Max Kreminski 2018, 23:09](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=1389)). Hannah Blair Salzman's Animal Crossing, where any task can be dropped without penalty, points toward the gardening side ([Hannah Blair Salzman 2022, 7:38](https://youtu.be/6GSXaM1PTMg?t=458)). A cozy roguelike that borrows the roguelite's resource loop sits close to this boundary; whether it feels like nurturing or like extraction depends on whether its world exists for its own sake or for the player's yield, and the talks do not settle where the line falls.

### Griefing: threat or content?

Leif Bloomquist treats abuse of shared objects as a threat to peers who need to progress, and his countermeasure became a bottleneck at about 40 players ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 12:01](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=721)). The Delve Bros treat viewers trolling the streamer as perhaps the most fun part of their game ([The Delve Bros 2020, 39:35](https://youtu.be/4jNMv79Xb6A?t=2375)). Which view holds depends on whether the target is a peer or a performer. The Delve Bros leave open how one game can serve both a streamer's crowd and a party of friends ([The Delve Bros 2020, 43:28](https://youtu.be/4jNMv79Xb6A?t=2608)), and how to keep individual success meaningful when a crowd solves a puzzle by brute force ([The Delve Bros 2020, 46:03](https://youtu.be/4jNMv79Xb6A?t=2763)). Gavin Verhey adds a further pull: he wants more co-op roguelikes, but endless replay makes a single-player mode critical ([Gavin Verhey 2024, 52:33](https://youtu.be/lGm8cZC8Lfk?t=3153)).

### Human referee or computer referee?

Jason Grinblat argues that tabletop play fails gracefully because people negotiate the rules, while a video game's framing simply fails ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 14:05](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=845)). Benjamin Berman points the other way for constant random handling, which a computer does far better than physical shuffling ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 32:34](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1954)), and Jon Perry finds the table's limits restrictive but freeing ([Jon Perry 2025, 29:40](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=1780)). Atty Vohra's rule resolves part of it: automate the parts of refereeing you find tedious and keep the parts you care about ([Atty Vohra 2021, 7:43](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=463)). How far automation should go is open; Vohra stops short of recommending a full world simulation ([Atty Vohra 2021, 9:47](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=587)).

### Generator as provocation, or hand-crafting?

Clarissa Littler and Max Hawkins treat a generator's job as moving a person off their habits, and Littler says the bar for that is low ([Clarissa Littler 2020, 10:00](https://youtu.be/OzCGTXakbjE?t=600); [Max Hawkins 2019, 7:59](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=479)); Chelsea Thompto adds that a single drop of randomness can be extremely powerful ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 2:34](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=154)). Nat Alison argues that generated sudoku grids bore because they are all solved the same way, and that only people have invented genuinely new rule combinations ([Nat Alison 2023, 2:14](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=134); [Nat Alison 2023, 7:57](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=477)). The positions agree that the novelty that matters comes from people, but they differ on what a generator's output is for. When the output is a stimulus for a maker, crude is fine; when it is the finished thing an audience consumes, variety of surface without variety of reasoning is not variety. Whether a generator could ever invent rules rather than arrange content, the thing Alison credits only to humans, the talks leave open.

### The price of the physical

Physical form buys things a screen cannot, and it charges for them. Hintline 93's paper binder cost more than an on-screen version, but having players flip pages under pressure felt close to the real job ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:40:05](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=24005)). A kneeling posture bought commitment from everyone who took it and excluded others, including the designer when injured ([G blekkenhorst 2026, 22:13](https://youtu.be/uZdEXqRkBZA?t=1333)). Manufacturers expect identical runs, which works against a generator's variety ([bleeptrack 2025, 4:22](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=262)). Each case trades reach for depth, and the talks give no general rule for where the line falls.

### Unsolved

- How do you stop evolution changing a living generative artwork? The Xenotext's host organism undid its gene ([Julian Day 2020, 24:45](https://youtu.be/aBbaUSWFQPM?t=1485)).
- Which theatre techniques, such as directing a scene's tone at a high level, could games adopt ([Nic Junius 2023, 33:34](https://youtu.be/cDxL6JoxYQc?t=2014))?
- Can bugs be understood as part of the intended experience rather than kept on a parallel track for speedrunners ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 5:44](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=344))?
- Which everyday activities, text-editor commands and other untapped verbs make good roguelikes ([Ludipe 2023, 10:29](https://youtu.be/pYtlU9wGopo?t=629); [Nick Bush 2026, 41:25](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=2485))?

## Checklist

1. Which structural element are you borrowing or exporting (the run, permanent loss, the container, a tagged generator, a short restartable session), and which are you deliberately dropping?
2. If you are adding game structure to an activity, are you enhancing what is already good about it, or turning it into points and badges?
3. For a hybrid, can you write down what each parent genre contributes, and would restricting yourself to those sources sharpen the design?
4. Are you choosing specific mechanics for what they do, rather than aiming for a ratio of roguelike to something else?
5. Which stretch of the source genre's play does your run contain, and why that one?
6. Does the source genre's feel keep players from experimenting, and does it reward routine or make-work you should remove?
7. On a new platform, have you planned a simplified variant rather than a port?
8. If you changed the subject, have you mapped every loop element to the new theme, and redesigned the rows where the equivalent has no reason to exist?
9. If the game moves to paper or a table, what carries generation, hidden state and the container, and which bookkeeping should stay on a computer?
10. Where can players' own invention feed back into the game?
11. With more than one player, is griefing a threat or the content, and have you tested your countermeasure at the real player count?
12. Can every participant see their contribution, or is success a lottery among the crowd?
13. In a physical space, does the information players need live in the room or on the screen, and who does a physical demand exclude?
14. If the output is an object, does it genuinely need its fabrication method, and does the generator emit the format the process needs?
15. Is your generator meant to finish the work or to provoke a person, and is it sized for that job?
